contentBlocks.title: Inflammation: definition and classification
contentBlocks.text: Inflammation is described in the textbook as the body's response to external stimuli, including microorganisms, physical injury and chemical exposure. In surgical practice, bacterial inflammation is emphasized. The source distinguishes acute from chronic inflammation, and specific from non-specific forms. Localized infection may remain in one site, while spread through the bloodstream can produce systemic infection.

contentBlocks.text: Core explanation

Inflammation is described in the textbook as the body's response to external stimuli, including microorganisms, physical injury and chemical exposure. In surgical practice, bacterial inflammation is emphasized. The source distinguishes acute from chronic inflammation, and specific from non-specific forms. Localized infection may remain in one site, while spread through the bloodstream can produce systemic infection.
How to study this section

Study the trigger, type, local response and general response as separate ideas. The textbook lists pain, swelling, redness, warmth and impaired function among local features; fever, chills, sweating, lethargy and a faster pulse among general features.

contentBlocks.title: Wounds: types, response and healing
contentBlocks.text: A wound is a break in the skin or deeper body-lining tissues and may follow injury, burns or surgery. The book groups wounds as closed, open, compound and surgical, and also notes whether they are clean, dirty or liable to contamination. Symptoms depend on the injury itself, the body's response and any later complication.

contentBlocks.text: Core explanation

The book groups wounds as closed, open, compound and surgical, and also notes whether they are clean, dirty or liable to contamination. Symptoms depend on the injury itself, the body's response and any later complication.
How to study this section

The healing sequence in the source is secretion, tissue formation and maturation. Healing may be delayed by devitalized tissue, poor nutrition, reduced local circulation, infection, radiation, fluid accumulation or repeated injury.

contentBlocks.title: Body water and fluid compartments
contentBlocks.text: The source states that water forms a major proportion of body weight and describes plasma, interstitial fluid and intracellular fluid as the principal compartments. It also explains that electrolytes are distributed differently inside and outside cells. Potassium, phosphate and bicarbonate are listed as important intracellular ions; sodium and chloride are emphasized extracellularly.

contentBlocks.caption: Chapter 2 — Fluids and Electrolytes • Body water and fluid compartments • Bawabet Al Tamreed

contentBlocks.text: Core explanation

The source states that water forms a major proportion of body weight and describes plasma, interstitial fluid and intracellular fluid as the principal compartments. It also explains that electrolytes are distributed differently inside and outside cells. Potassium, phosphate and bicarbonate are listed as important intracellular ions; sodium and chloride are emphasized extracellularly.
How to study this section

Understand the three compartments and the distinction between intracellular and extracellular electrolytes. The textbook includes numerical proportions; retain them as the source's teaching figures and be aware that estimates can vary by reference.
